observation_summary: The class ExtendedMessageFormat failed to override equals() and hashCode() methods, causing instances with different internal state (registry, pattern) to be considered equal or have identical hashcodes, violating the contract of these methods.
hypothesis: The class extends MessageFormat but fails to implement its own equals() and hashCode() methods to account for its additional fields (registry, toPattern). This leads to incorrect equality checks and hashcode collisions.
prediction: The fix will involve adding an @Override implementation of equals() and hashCode() that incorporates the class's specific fields into the comparison and hash calculation.
experiment_rationale: The provided diff shows the addition of both equals() and hashCode() methods to the ExtendedMessageFormat class, which correctly incorporate the class's unique fields (registry, toPattern) into the logic, confirming the hypothesis.
reasoning_summary: The defect is a failure to correctly implement the object equality and hashing contract for a subclass. While this is a structural issue, the fix is a procedural implementation of the required methods (the algorithm for equality and hashing). It is not a design-level capability omission (Function/Class/Object) because the class existed and functioned, but its internal logic for equality was incomplete/incorrect. It is not a Checking bug because it is not a missing guard, but a missing implementation of a standard method.
evidence_used: The bug report states: 'ExtendedMessageFormat doesn't override java.text.MessageFormat.equals(Object)'
The fix diff shows the addition of @Override equals(Object) and hashCode() methods.
The failing test 'testEqualsHashcode' confirms that the hashcode and equality logic were not behaving as expected for different registries.

alternative_types.why_not_primary: The class already existed and functioned; the issue was a missing implementation of standard methods (equals/hashCode) rather than a missing design-level capability.
While equality involves comparing objects, the root cause is the missing implementation of the equality algorithm within the class itself, not a broken association between two separate entities.
